idiom_name: hand-written consumer + mq_notify(SIGEV_THREAD) callback on a POSIX message queue
implementation_notes: C offers no listener structure, so the consumer is a hand-built struct - queue descriptor plus handler function - registered with mq_notify(); with SIGEV_THREAD the C library invokes sigev_notify_function on a thread it creates when a new message arrives on a previously empty queue, and with SIGEV_SIGNAL the handler runs in signal context. Because notification is one-shot and only one process may register per queue, the handler has to re-arm mq_notify() before draining (EBUSY otherwise), and the drain loop it runs is application code, not a library service. Hand-written primitives are justified for POSIX queues and embedded transports; everywhere else in C the same role is usually played by a socket event loop (select/poll/epoll) that dispatches ready descriptors to handler functions.
pitfalls: Notification fires only when a new message arrives on a queue that was empty and no thread is blocked in mq_receive(); messages already queued produce no callback, so drain explicitly.
One-shot registration: forgetting to re-arm mq_notify() makes the consumer go silently dormant - the classic failure of hand-written C consumers.
Only one process can register per queue; a second mq_notify() fails with EBUSY, and a blocked mq_receive() suppresses the notification entirely.

SIGEV_THREAD makes glibc create a thread (over a netlink socket) per notification - cheap for slow queues, costly under load; a SIGEV_SIGNAL handler runs in signal context and may only call async-signal-safe functions.
